# Norse mythology — provenance report

<!-- Generated from authored/norse-mythology.json by scripts/authored_decks.py. Do not edit: change the dossier and rebuild. -->

**Deck:** [`decks/norse-mythology.ttl`](../decks/norse-mythology.ttl) · **Cards:** 44 · **Licence:** [CC0 1.0 Universal](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/) · **Compiled by:** Anton Wiklund · **Created:** 2026-10-04

44 cards on Norse mythology as the Eddas tell it: the chief gods and what they rule or are known for (Thor → thunder), family ties the Eddas state (Loki's children Fenrir, Jörmungandr and Hel), Odin's horse, ravens and spear, Thor's hammer, the worlds of gods, humans and giants, Yggdrasil, Bifröst, Valhalla and Ragnarök. Front: a question; back: the answer, in English and Swedish, with the Swedish names in their established form (Oden, Tor, Mjölner). From the Prose and Poetic Eddas in public-domain translations and Wikidata, checked against Nationalencyklopedin and the Swedish Wikipedia.

## Licensing

The deck is CC0 1.0. Its content comes from three sources whose terms allow anything: the Prose Edda in Rasmus B. Anderson's translation (1879) and the Poetic Edda in Henry Adams Bellows's translation with his notes (1923), both public domain in the US (Project Gutenberg: "Public domain in the USA") and, since both translators died more than 70 years ago (1936 and 1939), also in countries with a term of life plus 70 years; and Wikidata, whose structured data is CC0, for the English and Swedish names and the statements. The selection of cards is our own (the gods, beings, places and events named in the editor's brief and attested in both Eddas), not taken from any list, and the questions, answers and notes are our own wording of facts; the quotations from the translations are in the evidence, as is allowed for public-domain texts in any case. Erik Brate's Swedish Poetic Edda (1913; Brate died in 1924) is also in the public domain and was used to verify the Swedish name forms; it also supplied the Swedish form Lodyn in one note. Nationalencyklopedin (all rights reserved; its texts may be quoted only non-commercially) and the Swedish Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0) were used for verification only: they confirmed the Swedish names and facts the content sources gave, and no wording or selection was taken from them, apart from two single Swedish name forms that the Swedish Wikipedia supplied or confirmed (Jord, also written so in Anderson's translation, and Jörmungand), which are facts and not protected wording; the short passages quoted from them in the provenance report are evidence for the checks, not part of the cards. The CC0 dedication covers the cards only. The quotations from Nationalencyklopedin and the Swedish Wikipedia in the provenance report are short verbatim quotations with their source named, used as evidence under the right of quotation (upphovsrättslagen 22 §) and, for Wikipedia, under CC BY-SA 4.0 with the article and revision cited; they are not released under CC0.

## Method

1. Who did the work: Anton Wiklund compiled this deck with the help of AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic), which did the research, drafting and cross-checking at his direction. The cards were checked by machine (a script that matched every quotation word for word against the saved source texts, live Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators) and in independent review rounds by further Claude agents, each logged under Quality control with its findings and how they were resolved. Anton Wiklund reviews every deck in full before it is released.
2. 1. Texts. The two Eddas were downloaded as plain text from Project Gutenberg (queries 1–2): the Prose Edda in Rasmus B. Anderson's translation (1879, eBook #18947), which covers Gylfaginning in full and the main passages of Skáldskaparmál, and the Poetic Edda in Henry Adams Bellows's translation with his notes (1923, eBook #73533). Both translators died more than 70 years ago (Wikidata, query 3). Anderson numbers the paragraphs of Gylfaginning (§1–§59); the locators use those numbers. Bellows's locators name the poem and the stanza, or the note to a stanza.
3. 2. Selection. The cards cover what the editor's brief asked for, as far as both Eddas attest it: the chief gods and what Gylfaginning says each rules or is known for (§20–§33), the family ties stated in the Eddas, Odin's and Thor's best-known possessions, the beings and worlds of the creation story, Yggdrasil, Bifröst, Valhalla and the main events of Ragnarök (§55–§56, Voluspo 44–56). Each candidate fact was kept only if Anderson's Prose Edda states it and, wherever the poems cover it, Bellows's Poetic Edda agrees; see Selection for what was left out.
4. 3. Wikidata. The items were found by their English Wikipedia titles (API call 4, wbgetentities with sites=enwiki), which returned the English, Swedish and multilingual labels and aliases, the Swedish Wikipedia sitelinks and every statement of the items; the labels of the statements' values were fetched in a second call (API call 5). Two exploratory searches by name (wbsearchentities, query 6) came first. The English names on the cards are the Wikidata English label, or an English alias where the label differs from the form the Eddas' translators and the English Wikipedia use (Baldr rather than the label Baldur; Idun, Vidar, Huginn and Muninn); the Swedish names are the Wikidata Swedish label or alias, except where step 4 says otherwise.
5. 4. Swedish. Every Swedish name was compared with the headword of Nationalencyklopedin's article (query 7: the free opening of each article, saved with its URL), with the title of the Swedish Wikipedia article (query 8: the introductions and revision ids, API) and, for names in the poems, with Erik Brate's Swedish Poetic Edda of 1913 (query 9, Project Runeberg). They agree on Oden, Tor, Balder, Loke, Frej, Freja, Njord, Tyr, Heimdall, Idun, Brage, Frigg, Vidar, Höder, Hel, Fenrisulven, Midgårdsormen, Sleipner, Mjölner, Hugin och Munin, Gungner, Bifrost, Yggdrasil, Valhall, Ragnarök, Asgård, Midgård, Jotunheim, Muspelhem, Nifelhem, Surt, Ymer, Mimer and valkyria. NE has no article on Angerboda or Gleipner (the addresses answered with an error page); for these the Swedish Wikipedia titles and the Wikidata Swedish labels agree, and NE's article on Fenrisulven writes "jättekvinnan Angerboda". Thor's mother has no Swedish Wikidata label of her own (the item's Swedish label is "Fjorgyn"); the Swedish form Jord is from the Swedish Wikipedia article Tor ("son till ”allfadern” Oden och asynjan Jord") and Thor's Swedish Wikidata alias "Jords son". Her other names in the card's note are Anderson's English forms Fjorgyn and Hlodyn (Vocabulary and §56); the Swedish forms Fjorgyn and Lodyn are Brate's (Völuspå 56, "Lodyns" and "Fjorgyns son"; query 12), Fjorgyn also being the Wikidata Swedish label and the Swedish Wikipedia title (which writes the other name Lödyn). The Swedish questions and answers were written by the compiler following NE's and Swedish Wikipedia's usage: asarna in lower case, Snorres Edda for the Prose Edda, Ragnarök with a capital as in NE and Wikidata (Brate writes ragnarök). Names in the notes: Jörmungand from the Swedish Wikipedia article Midgårdsormen ("Jörmungand (Jǫrmungandr"; Wikidata's Swedish aliases have only Jörmundgand and similar forms); Svadilfare from the Wikidata Swedish label of Q1125073 and the Swedish Wikipedia article Svadilfare; Ivaldes söner from Anderson's "the sons of Ivalde" (§44) with the Swedish genitive, as NE also writes it (Wikidata's Q37499380 has the Swedish label Ivaldi). The English form Ivaldi in the same note is Bellows's (Grimnismol 43, "Ivaldi’s sons", and his note to it).
6. 5. Cross-check. Every card was checked against at least two sources: the Prose Edda (Anderson) and, where the poems cover the fact, the Poetic Edda (Bellows), plus Wikidata (names and, where it has them, the statement) and Nationalencyklopedin, or the Swedish Wikipedia where NE has no article or does not cover the fact. The evidence of each card quotes what each source says. The script make_dossier.py (query 10) wrote this dossier from the card data: it checks that every quoted passage occurs word for word in the saved copy of its source (the Gutenberg and Runeberg texts, the NE openings and the Wikipedia extracts; in the NE openings, the spaces that removing the HTML tags left before punctuation and inside brackets are removed before comparing and quoting), prints where each Anderson and Bellows quotation stands (chapter, poem, stanza or note) so that the locators could be compared by hand, and writes the Wikidata evidence of each card from its checks and the saved entities, failing if the saved data do not satisfy a check. The scripts themselves are not published; the rules above are what they do.
7. 6. Cards. Fronts are questions in English and Swedish; backs are a name or a short phrase in our own words, with a short note where it helps (for example the meaning of the ravens' names, or how a death at Ragnarök comes about). The answers about what a god rules follow the Prose Edda's own words, shortened: Njord "rules the course of the wind and checks the fury of the sea" → the wind and the sea (the card's note adds that he also checks the fury of fire, so a learner who knows the whole sentence is not misled); Freyr "rules over rain and sunshine, and over the fruits of the earth". English names follow one convention: the familiar anglicised forms of the English translations and of Wikidata's English labels and aliases, written without the Old Norse letter ð and without acute accents (Njord, Tyr, Idun, Vidar, Jord, Angrboda, Hodr, Mimir, Svadilfari), keeping ö only in the four names English usually writes with it (Mjölnir, Jörmungandr, Bifröst, Ragnarök) and the nominative -r where English keeps it (Freyr, Surtr, Huginn). Where an English and a Swedish name differ only in convention, each language has its own form (Baldr/Balder, Fenrir/Fenrisulven, Jörmungandr/Midgårdsormen). Study direction front to back only: several answers recur (Loki answers three cards, Fenrir and Jörmungandr two each), and many fronts are descriptions that would not make sense as answers.
8. 7. Machine checks. For every card the builder checks against live Wikidata that the English and Swedish names on the card are labels or aliases of the item (except where noted in quality control, such as Hodr) and, where Wikidata has the statement, the fact itself: Thor is a thunder deity (P31 Q842697), Freyja a love deity (P31 Q1670614), Tyr's domain is war, Bragi's poetry, Freyr's weather and Loki's deception (P2925); Thor's mother is Jord, Baldr's parents Odin and Frigg, Njord's children Freyr and Freyja, Angrboda's and Loki's children Fenrir, Jörmungandr and Hel, Sleipnir's mother Loki (P22, P25, P26, P40); Mjölnir is Thor's and Sleipnir and Gungnir Odin's (P127); Odin is killed by Fenrir, Fenrir by Vidar, Thor and Jörmungandr by each other, Baldr by Hodr, Freyr by Surtr and Ymir by Odin (P157); Bifröst is made of the rainbow (P186). Facts Wikidata does not record (Odin's eye, Tyr's hand, Heimdall and Loki killing each other, Idun's apples, the worlds' descriptions) rest on the Eddas and the cross-check in step 5. The built deck was validated with the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators (validate_sources.ts).

## Selection

44 cards: 11 on the chief gods and what the Prose Edda says they rule or are known for (Odin, Thor, Baldr, Njord, Freyr, Freyja, Tyr, Bragi, Heimdall, Idun, Loki); 8 on family ties stated in the Eddas (Thor's mother Jord, Baldr's parents Odin and Frigg, Njord as father of Freyr and Freyja, Loki's children with Angrboda — Fenrir, Jörmungandr and Hel — and Loki as the mother of Sleipnir); 8 on beings and things (Mjölnir, Sleipnir, Huginn and Muninn, Gungnir, Gleipnir, the valkyries, Ymir, Surtr); 9 on the world (Yggdrasil, Bifröst, Valhalla, Asgard, Midgard, Jotunheim, Muspelheim, Niflheim, Ragnarök); and 8 on stories (Odin's eye, Tyr's hand, the death of Baldr, and who kills whom at Ragnarök). Included only what the Eddas themselves state, with nothing from later retellings, folklore or modern popular culture. Left out: the list of the nine worlds, which neither Edda gives (Bellows's note to Voluspo 2 lists eight and calls the ninth "uncertain"), and with it Vanaheim, Alfheim, Svartalfheim and Nidavellir; minor gods and goddesses about whom the Eddas say little (Ull, Forseti, Vali, Hermod, Sif, Nanna, Sigyn, Skadi and the goddesses of Gylfaginning §36) and Frigg, apart from her place as Baldr's mother; claims on which the sources differ, such as Tyr's father (Odin in Snorri, the giant Hymir in Hymiskvitha), Heimdall's mothers or the fate of Mimir's head; and interpretations that are not in the Eddas (Odin as god of war or of the dead, Freyr and Freyja as fertility gods, Loki as a fire god), although the notes keep the Eddas' own statements, such as Freyja's half of the slain. Thor's link to thunder is given by his name and by both translators (Bellows: "the thunder-god"; Anderson's vocabulary: "The god of thunder"), not spelled out in Snorri's description of him, which calls him the strongest of gods and men; the card keeps the universally used answer "thunder" and gives Snorri's description in the note.

## Quality control

6 rounds, 37 findings: 29 fixed, 1 rejected after checking, 7 needing no change. Every card's Wikidata checks (128 in all) are re-run against live Wikidata by `scripts/authored_decks.py check` before every build.

### Round 0: Sources, licences and machine checks: every card against Anderson's Prose Edda and, where the poems cover it, Bellows's Poetic Edda; the names and statements against Wikidata; the Swedish names against Nationalencyklopedin, the Swedish Wikipedia and Brate's Swedish Edda; every quotation verified word for word against the saved texts by make_dossier.py. (2026-10-04)

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — authoring agent, machine checks · **Scope:** All 44 cards, the sources and their licences, and the deck metadata.

Every card is stated in the Prose Edda, and every card the poems cover agrees with the Poetic Edda; Wikidata agrees with the Eddas wherever it has the statement, and NE or the Swedish Wikipedia confirms every Swedish name. No Wikidata check was skipped because Wikidata disagreed with the Eddas; the findings below are differences in naming, gaps in Wikidata or the reference works, and facts left out because the sources differ.

|---|---|---|---|
